newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew, facing risky repairs, try to save energy.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew, facing risky repairs, try to save energy.

text.p: The crippled Mir space station was stable on Friday but mission control warned its weary Russian and American astronauts to conserve their energy before attempting risky repair work.
"The situation has stabilised," deputy mission chief Sergei Krikalyov told reporters at Korolyov Mission Control near Moscow two days after the worst accident of Mir's 11 years in space.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39, and American physicist Michael Foale, 40, sounded calm in conversations with mission control but were showing signs of fatigue.

They face a tough task trying to restore vital electric power supplies from the Spektr scientific module, holed by a cargo craft during docking manoeuvres on Wendesday. That work will start when new equipment arrives in about 10 days.
"The crew told us that entering the Spektr will be difficult. We advised them not to waste their strength," Krikalyov said.
One Russian official said the crew were "experiencing emotional and physical stress" and had been told to rest. "When do we get time to sleep?" one of the cosmonauts was heard asking.

Krikalyov told the two Russians they would have to put on spacesuits while Foale sits in the escape capsule for safety as they do the repair work. "It's very problematic," one of the Russian cosmonauts replied.
The repair mission will require special adapters for the cosmonauts' space suits and a special airtight door device, being manufactured this weekend.
Both pieces of equipment will be delivered with other supplies aboard an unmanned Progress cargo craft to be launched on July 4 or July 5. The trip to Mir should take about two days.
Until then, their electricity supply cut by about a half after Spektr and its four power-generating solar panels were sealed off, there is not much the three cosmonauts can do.
Many of the station's systems have been shut down, experiments are halted and they are not allowed to exert themselves, to save air and power.

Mir is hotter, clammier and darker than usual, making for a long, bleak wait for help. Officials say they are in no immediate danger and can always take to the "lifeboat" -- the three-man Soyuz TM escape module moored alongside.
Russian officials say they do not want the crew to evacuate, which could spell the end for the world's only orbital station.
The next Mir crew, Anatoly Solovyov, Pavel Vinogradov and the Frenchman Leopold Eyharts, has begun training and could continue the repairs after their scheduled arrival in August.

Eyharts' mission is part of a European cooperation deal on Mir which, with NASA, has bankrolled the cash-strapped Russian cosmos programme since the end of the Cold War space race. Mir has been a test-bed for the international space station Alpha, the first section of which Russia is due to launch next year.

The latest accident, rated a "five" on Russia's seven-point space emergency scale, follows a serious fire in February and a host of other mishaps and financial problems that have sparked calls in Washington for NASA to dump the Russians.

However, the head of NASA's Mir programme Frank Culbertson said it was too soon to consider the future of NASA's missions to Mir, saying an end to supply trips by the U.S. space shuttle would make it hard for the station to survive.

If Mir were abandoned, recalling memories of the nearly disastrous mission of the U.S. Apollo 13 in 1970, the world's governments would also face a 140-tonne headache. Mir could drift back toward Earth and, since it is far too big to burn up in the atmosphere, it could fall on a built-up area.
The long wait will also be a test for the crew's families.

Tsibliyev's wife Larisa told a Russian newspaper her husband's intensive survival training in extreme situations would pull him through the ordeal. If that was not enough, he was carrying a plastic rabbit given to him by their daughter.
"It may not be pretty, but it always works," she said.
